newsitem.title: USA: Philip Morris buyback boosts stock price.
newsitem.headline: Philip Morris buyback boosts stock price.

text.p: A renewed share repurchase plan and a three-for-one stock split by Philip Morris Cos Inc Wednesday helped boost the company's stock and prompted Wall Street analysts to repeat buy recommendations.
Analysts agreed that with Philip Morris shares trading in the 130's the repurchases will cost more than in the past, but they said they are still a good value.
"It will be additive to per-share earnings immediately," said Emanuel Goldman, PaineWebber Group Inc analyst.

At one point Wednesday Philip Morris shares traded $3.50 higher than the previous close, but they gave up some of the gain in later trading with the overall stock market reeling after a warning from Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan about the sustainability of sharp gains in stock prices.
Philip Morris was up 1/2 to 133-3/4 about 30 minutes before the end of New York Stock Exchange trading. The Dow industrials were off 80 to 6959 at that point.
John Maxwell, analyst at Wheat First Butcher Singer, said the buyback was a good move because the stock was "bloody cheap."
Maxwell said he has an "aggressive buy" rating on Philip Morris.
PaineWebber's Goldman said he is keeping a buy rating on Philip Morris because he considers the stock cheap even as it trades near its 12-month high.
Martin Feldman, analyst at Smith Barney Inc, said he has an "aggressive buy" rating on the stock and thinks the share price could reach 145 by the end of 1997.
But Feldman said the stock could be volatile as it responds to news of developments in anti-tobacco lawsuits.

Goldman said when anti-tobacco plaintiffs had a federal class-action suit in New Orleans decertified, it was a big blow to them. "Decertification really worsened the economics for the plaintiffs' bar," Goldman said.
He said plaintiffs now had to pursue their cases state by state, which is more expensive. He said rumors about settlement talks may have come from the plaintiffs' side.
"The likelihood of a near-term settlement is minuscule," he said.
Feldman said a settlment would have to be accompanied by federal legislation and that would take a long time.

On Wednesday, a spokesman for the tobacco industry, responding to a question, said no negotiations were under way. "No one has presented a proposal to the industry nor has the industry presented a proposal," spokeman Lance Morgan said. He said he was reiterating a comment made a week ago.
Goldman said the bullish case for Philip Morris was that the company generated free cash flow of about $340,000 an hour, and that money was available for repurchases.
With the stock trading at a modest price/earnings ratio, the buybacks are good value for the company and for shareholders, he said.
